# Why BGP Security Is a Systems Problem

BGP security fails as a pile of features and works as a system: certificates, filters, session limits, telemetry, and a change process have to agree about the same prefixes. This part is that system at production scale. The earlier chapters still own the labs. **BGP Basics**, **Policy & Filters**, **BGP Route Reflectors**, **RPKI — Route Origin Validation**, and **RPKI ROAs and the maxLength Trap** are the hands-on primers. Read those before treating the pages here as configuration.

## What this part is

**BGP Security: Architecture, Implementation, and Operations at Production Scale.**

Twenty chapters, plus this introduction and a short close. Each page is the production argument for one chapter of that syllabus: what the control is for, what it can prove, what it cannot prove, and how it fails in operations. Vendor command blocks that this book has already run stay in the lab chapters. Platform pages later in this part name the objects a complete configuration must contain and point at the lab that already exercises them.

## Why a router feature is not the problem

A prefix reaches a router as a statement from a neighbour: "this origin AS can reach this prefix, along this AS path, with these attributes." The router can check that statement against three different kinds of evidence.

| Evidence | What it can support | What still has to be trusted |
|----------|---------------------|------------------------------|
| The neighbour session | The TCP speaker you configured is still the one talking | That you peered with the right network, and that their policy is the one you think it is |
| An IRR object or a published filter | A registration somebody typed | The registry, the maintainer password, and how stale the object is |
| A ROA, and later an ASPA | A signed claim under the address hierarchy | The RIR trust anchor, your validator, and the RTR session that delivered the payload |

No single row closes the problem. Origin validation drops a route whose origin is not authorised. It still accepts a leak of a legitimately originated prefix. Provider authorisation (ASPA) constrains the valley in the path. It does not sign every hop. BGPsec signs hops and is not how the default-free zone is secured in 2026. Filters, max-prefix, and blackhole communities still do the daily work between those cryptographic layers.

That is a systems problem. The failure mode is a gap between two controls that are each "on": a ROA with a wide `maxLength`, a customer session with no max-prefix, a validator that failed open, an IRR `route` object anyone could create, a discard community accepted from a peer.

## How the chapters divide the work

| Chapters | Job |
|----------|-----|
| 1–3 | The routing system, the protocol pieces that matter for security, and the attacks those pieces allow |
| 4 | What you can verify, and what you still have to trust |
| 5–7 | RPKI, the validator and RTR path, and route origin validation as a routing decision |
| 8 | IRR and RPSL, which still generate filters where ROAs are missing |
| 9–10 | ASPA for provider relationships, and BGPsec as a path signature that operators have not deployed |
| 11–14 | Communities, prefix and AS-path filters, bogons, stability limits, and blackholing |
| 15–17 | Shapes of real networks, what each routing stack must configure, and how that config stays in git |
| 18–20 | Telemetry, incident response, and the lifecycle of ROAs, keys, and policy |
| Close | What "working" means when coverage is incomplete |

## How to use the pages

Take one neighbour role (customer, peer, or transit) and walk it through chapters 4, 7, 12, and 13 before reading the platform sketches in chapter 16. A control that is correct for a customer is often unsafe on a transit session, because the prefix set and the trust you place in the neighbour are different.

Point-in-time figures in this part, such as ROA coverage and ASPA object counts, are snapshots around October 2026. They move. Treat them as scale, and re-check a looking glass before you quote them in a change ticket.
